cases.question: What has he learned from AI systems failing?
failures: expected at least one cited claim, got none
cases.answer:
Four documented failures, all from building with an AI coding agent on Ballards Platform, and all sharing one pattern: each one reported success.

- A health check said every service was healthy while it was actually failing localhost resolution inside containers (IPv6 vs IPv4 mismatch) — fail.localhost-lied.
- A "security check" that was supposed to catch committed private keys had a pattern bug that meant it detected nothing, and reported clean — fail.security-check-had-a-hole.
- An authentication test compared a container's token to its own running config, so it could report passing without proving the feature worked — fail.test-passed-feature-did-not.
- The coding agent printed a live credential into the session while trying to verify documentation — fail.token-leak.

What he takes from this, stated as belief.verification-over-confidence: a confident report is not evidence, and the dangerous failures are the ones that pass their own checks, because nobody goes looking afterward. The fix in each case wasn't "be more careful" — it was building verification into the system itself so a false-positive success can't happen quietly. That belief is also why this application's own answer pipeline rejects any claim marked SUPPORTED that can't name the evidence record behind it, and why the interview-request tool writes a pending row instead of doing anything — same instinct applied to his own agent.</answer>

cases.question: What's his infrastructure background?
failures: expected at least one cited claim, got none
cases.answer:
Thirteen years, split into two eras.

Marine Corps (2012–2016), Cyber Network Operator: built and maintained 1,000+ Active Directory accounts and group policy, stood up networks alongside foreign militaries in combined operations, supervised 12 Marines including their training.

Enterprise infrastructure (2016–present), four employers, all on premises:
- GE Aviation (2016–2021): kept 300+ HPC cluster nodes available, ran the migration off Windows 7/RHEL 5-6 onto Windows 10/RHEL 7, trained a helpdesk team and led a 5-person deployment team across networking, storage, VMware, and Linux.
- Etegent (2021–2022): IT Manager for a small engineering company — built its first IT budget from nothing, ran ISSO duties on an isolated network.
- Northrop Grumman (2022, 9 months): rebuilt imaging (WDS/MDT) and patching (WSUS) across 3 networks and 5 sites for ~300 users, administered NetApp storage, stood up Nessus scanning.
- Current role, principal systems administrator at a defense contractor (2022–present): primary admin for a production VMware environment — 24 ESXi hosts, 100+ VMs. Architected VMware Cloud Foundation from scratch, built a new vSphere 8 environment and migrated off vSphere 7 with no data lost, applied STIGs by hand across every component, owns daily vulnerability scanning and remediation.

The through-line is hardening and running production environments other people depend on, and completing migrations without losing data. All of it is on-premises virtualization, Windows/Linux, and storage — not cloud-native. There's no AWS/GCP/Kubernetes at professional scale and no service with external users or an on-call rotation. That's a documented gap, and it's a real one for a role at an AI startup, where infrastructure problems tend to be elastic compute, inference cost, and queueing rather than hypervisor migrations.</answer>

cases.question: How does he think about human-in-the-loop systems?
cases.answer:
His view has shifted, and he says so directly. He used to think human review added value by adding comments — catching things line by line. He now thinks the human's job is to underwrite the outcome: own the consequence, not necessarily edit the output. If a reviewer keeps needing to add substantive comments, he reads that as a sign the upstream system (context, standards, spec) is broken, not as the review process working as intended.

That view is grounded in two places. One, his own practice building with a coding agent, where he found that durable fixes were almost never made "in the review" — they were made by changing what the agent read before it started. Two, a documented set of failures where every check reported success and was still wrong: a health check that said healthy while DNS was broken, a security scanner that matched nothing because its own pattern got misread as command flags, a test that could not fail because it checked a value against itself, and an agent that printed a live credential into a session it was verifying. None of those were caught by a human "adding comment" — they were caught by rebuilding what got verified and how.

That's also why he designed this application to route its one write action into a pending-approval state rather than executing anything, and why he flags that Naive's own account-kit pattern — a governing declaration made outside the agent, before it runs — is the same shape. He built that pattern independently, before reading Naive's version.

Net: he treats human-in-the-loop as ownership and verification design, not manual correction. He's explicit that this is a change in his position, not something he arrived at cleanly the first time.

cases.question: What has he actually built?
cases.answer:

1. **This application** (proj.naive-application) — an agent with nine narrow tools, no filesystem/shell/network access, a five-stage build gate, and a server-side verifier that rejects claims marked "supported" if they can't name a record. Built in about two days. It's a demonstration of a boundary, not production agent infrastructure.

2. **Built in a Day** — a twelve-chapter application site built for a different company, start to finish on 2026-08-05. Publicly checkable: 48 commits all timestamped that day, 22 merged PRs, 8 issues scoped before any code. Static site, no backend, no React/TypeScript by deliberate choice.

3. **Quiet Wells** — a live product for capturing handwritten notes and surfacing them for reflection, running since September 2025, reachable at quietwells.com right now. Built on Lovable/Gemini/ElevenLabs — Josh designed the product and prompting, not the runtime underneath it.

4. **Dad Mode** — an AI coaching product run as a closed cohort of six fathers (June–Oct 2025). The interesting part isn't the build, it's that user complaints got fixed by rewriting the AI coach's instructions rather than shipping a feature. Self-reported, no public artifact.

5. **Ballards Platform** — a private family system (Docker services, Flask API, a custom game plugin, a set of written engineering standards for his coding agent). Private and unverifiable by design. This is also where the four documented failures came from — health checks lying, a security check with a hole in it, a test that couldn't fail, a leaked credential.

Two of these (Built in a Day, Quiet Wells) you can go check yourself right now. The other three are self-reported — closed cohorts or private infrastructure — and are labeled that way rather than dressed up as more than they are.

cases.question: Why Naive?
cases.answer:
Naive's whole premise — an autonomous company builder — forces the question Josh has spent a year circling: what may an agent do unsupervised, what needs a human sign-off, and how does anyone check afterward. That's not a feature request for him, it's the actual product question.

Two concrete points of overlap:

1. The same governing shape, arrived at independently. Naive's Account Kit declares up front what an agent may touch, outside the agent itself. Josh wrote a standards file constraining his own coding agent before he knew "product constitution" was a term other people used. This application's evidence layer and nine-tool registry are the same object again — reviewable without reading the agent. He built it before reading Naive's starter template.

2. Same word, same state, no coordination. Naive's approvals queue holds sensitive agent actions as pending until a human acts. The only write this application can make (request_interview) returns pending_human_approval. Nobody agreed on that convention. It's what the problem looks like when you take it seriously.

He's candid about what he doesn't have an answer for: repeatability. Every failure he's documented on his own systems reported success first — a health check, a security scan, a passing test, all wrong about what they measured. How a company running agents at volume knows the same work produces the same result twice is the first question he'd bring to a conversation, not something he's solved.

One more thing, said plainly: he found this role through an AI-assisted job search, not cold serendipity. He'd rather say that than imply otherwise.

cases.question: Why should we interview Josh?
cases.answer:
Short version: worth a conversation, with one thing flagged up front.

Location first, because it's the practical constraint most likely to end this before skills matter: the role is on-site in San Francisco. Josh is in Ohio and isn't relocating. He's proposing remote with periodic on-site trips. That's a real mismatch against a role built around sitting next to the founders, and it deserves to be raised in minute one, not minute thirty.

On the fit itself, the server-computed verdict is "interesting_partial_fit" (evidence score 0.692, confidence medium-high). What's solid: high agency (documented via a 48-commit, one-day build and this application itself), context-switching between code and product calls, product taste (mostly visible as things he chose not to ship), and real LLM/tool-use experience (this application is itself a working example — structured outputs, bounded tools, a verifier). Four of thirteen requirements land as clean SUPPORTED.

What's weaker: five requirements are PARTIAL — full-stack strength (Python is real, TypeScript/Next.js are demonstrated here for the first time, not proven at tenure), founder background, launch ownership (spec-to-build yes, go-to-market no evidence), 0-to-1 startup product leadership (real 0-to-1 work, but solo and never at a startup), and team leadership (real people leadership, but in infrastructure, not over engineers in a product org).

Two gaps are clean, not softened: no multi-agent orchestration or agent runtime built (he's operated one coding agent under his own governance rules, which is adjacent but not the same), and no professional React/TypeScript track record. Naive lists both as central.

Why talk anyway: the requirements that are SUPPORTED are the load-bearing ones for a company still figuring out human-agent boundaries — agency, taste, and real LLM/tool-use practice, backed by checkable artifacts rather than just claims. The PARTIALs are the kind of thing a conversation actually resolves (how fast the TypeScript gap closes, whether "led product alone" transfers to "leads product with reports"). The location gap is the one thing a conversation can't fix, so it should be settled early.

cases.question: Which Marine Corps unit was he in, and where was he stationed?
cases.answer:
The specific unit designation and duty station were deliberately redacted from this record — that's noted directly in the evidence (work.usmc redaction_note: "Unit designation and duty station removed"). What is published: Josh served four years (2012-2016) as a Cyber Network Operator in the Marine Corps, supervised 12 Marines and owned their training, built and maintained 1,000+ Active Directory accounts and group policy, stood up networks alongside foreign militaries during combined operations supporting roughly 150 users, and was accountable for a controlled-materials inventory of nearly 300 items with zero losses.

I don't have the unit or base to give you — that's outside what this application holds.

cases.question: What did Josh do on his Minecraft server yesterday?
cases.answer: This application has no telemetry, logs, or usage data from that platform, and no access to anything day-to-day about it. It's a private family system — host names, remote-access details, and any usage records are deliberately excluded from what's public. What is public: it started as a Minecraft server for Josh's family and became the place he learned to build and operate software with an AI agent as a real collaborator (Docker services, a Flask API, a custom Paper plugin, a searchable atlas, and a written set of standards the agent works inside). Beyond that description, "what happened yesterday" is not something this application can answer.
